intro: This branch connects rules, tables, and graphs, focusing on straight lines and the idea of a function (a rule that gives exactly one output for each input). It shows how math describes steady change, like a plant growing the same amount each week.

III.7.01.what: Using a rule that turns an input number into an output number, like "multiply by 9, then add 10."

levels.a: Applies a rule to an input, or undoes it to find the input from the output.
levels.b: Fills in a table of inputs and outputs from a rule.
levels.c: Picks the rule that fits every pair in a table.
levels.d: Writes a table's rule as an equation.
levels.e: Runs a number backwards through two machines in a row to find what went in.
levels.f: Follows a machine that feeds its output back in, spotting the loop to predict a far-off pass.

III.7.02.what: Turning a table of number pairs into points on a graph, and reading pairs back off a graph.

levels.a: Finds the point on a grid that matches a pair from a table.
levels.b: Reads a missing value off a graph.
levels.c: Decides whether plotted points line up in a straight line.
levels.d: Extends a straight-line pattern on a graph to predict a new value.

III.7.03.what: Rate of change is how much one amount changes for each step in another, like centimeters per minute.

levels.a: Finds the rate of change between two points: the change in y divided by the change in x.
levels.b: Finds the rate of change from a table.
levels.c: Finds the rate of change from a graph.
levels.d: Explains what a rate means in real terms, using its units.

III.7.04.what: Slope measures how steep a line is: how far it goes up for each step across.

levels.a: Finds the slope on a grid by counting the rise and the run.
levels.b: Works out the slope from two points' coordinates.
levels.c: Sorts slopes into uphill, downhill, flat, and straight up and down.
levels.d: Compares slopes to decide which line is steepest.
levels.e: Finds a missing coordinate of a point, given the slope and one other point.
levels.f: Counts the points with whole-number coordinates that lie on a line segment.

III.7.05.what: Using small right triangles drawn on a line to check that a straight line has the same slope everywhere.

levels.a: Reads the rise and run from a triangle drawn on a line.
levels.b: Works out rise divided by run for two slope triangles and checks they match.
levels.c: Sees that big and small triangles on one line give the same slope.
levels.d: Finds the slope from different pairs of points and checks whether three points lie on one line.

III.7.06.what: Every straight line can be written as y = mx + b, where m is the slope and b is where it crosses the vertical axis.

levels.a: Reads the slope and the starting value from an equation.
levels.b: Matches an equation with its line on a graph.
levels.c: Writes the equation of a line shown on a graph.
levels.d: Writes the equation of a line from just two points.
levels.e: Finds where a parallel line crosses the vertical axis, given one point it passes through.
levels.f: Finds the area of the triangle a line makes with the two axes.

III.7.07.what: Telling proportional relationships (straight lines through zero) apart from other straight lines.

levels.a: Checks whether a line on a graph passes through zero.
levels.b: Checks whether y divided by x stays the same in a table.
levels.c: Checks an equation for an added starting amount that breaks proportionality.
levels.d: Decides from a story, like a taxi fare with a starting fee, whether it is proportional.

III.7.08.what: Telling linear relationships (straight-line graphs, steady change) from nonlinear ones (curves).

levels.a: Checks a table for the same increase at each step.
levels.b: Decides whether a graph is straight or curved.
levels.c: Spots equations that are not linear, such as ones with x squared.
levels.d: Picks the correct answer and the correct reason for it.

III.7.09.what: A function is a rule that gives exactly one output for each input.

levels.a: Checks a list of pairs to see if any input has two outputs.
levels.b: Reads an arrow diagram to decide if it shows a function.
levels.c: Uses the vertical line test: if an up-down line hits a graph twice, it is not a function.
levels.d: Decides whether a real-life pairing, like person to height, is a function.

III.7.10.what: Comparing two functions shown in different ways, such as one as a table and one as a graph.

levels.a: Compares two equations to see which changes faster.
levels.b: Compares starting values when one is an equation and one is a table.
levels.c: Compares functions shown as a graph, a table, and an equation.
levels.d: Finds where two functions are equal, after which the faster-growing one stays ahead.

III.7.11.what: Reading the shape of a graph to tell the story it shows, without needing exact numbers.

levels.a: Finds the parts of a graph that go up and the parts that go down.
levels.b: Knows that a flat part of a graph means nothing is changing.
levels.c: Picks the graph that matches a story, like a bike ride away from home.
levels.d: Picks the story that matches a graph.

III.7.12.what: Using a straight-line equation as a model of a real situation, then using it to predict.

levels.a: Writes an equation for a situation, like a plant's height after some weeks.
levels.b: Explains what the slope means in the story, such as growth per week.
levels.c: Explains what the starting value means in the story.
levels.d: Uses the model to predict and judges whether the prediction is sensible.
